newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: OPINION - THE ROLE OF INSTITUTIONS - BY TONY HAWKINS.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - THE ROLE OF INSTITUTIONS - BY TONY HAWKINS.

text.p: By Tony Hawkins, Professor of Business Studies at The University of Zimbabwe
Last week's publication of the World Bank's 1997 World Development Report highlights a long-neglected area of crucial importance for African economic development - the role of institutions.

Many in the donor community challenge the assertion that they have neglected institutional development, pointing to the vast amounts of foreign aid devoted to technical assistance and "capacity-building".

But the proof of the pudding is in the eating or, more accurately, in the behaviour of governments like those of the U.S., pushing for trade and private foreign investment rather than aid, and the World Development Report itself, noting that "in aid-dependent countries donors sometimes alleviate, but too often worsen, the problem of weak central capacity".

According to the World Bank the deterioration in the state's effectiveness has been most severe in sub-Saharan Africa - "the result of eroding civil service wages, heavy dependence on aid and patronage politics".

Of course the donor community, including the Bank itself and the IMF, must carry the can, at least partially, for two of those problems. In Zimbabwe for instance, civil service real earnings plunged 30% between 1991 and 1995, during which period an IMF/World Bank reform programme was being implemented. A feature of the report is its use of a survey of business opinion - 3,685 firms in some 69 countries, including nearly 1,300 firms in 22 sub-Saharan countries.

The survey asked businesspeople to rank the relative importance of eight distinct obstacles to economic activity, thereby pinpointing those areas of government activity where improvement is most needed.

In Sub-Saharan Africa, corruption is ranked as the top obstacle (in Latin America also), followed by taxes and infrastructure. Inflation is cited as the fourth most serious problem followed by crime and theft, the availability and cost of finance, policy instability with, perhaps surprisingly, government regulation as the least serious of the eight problems.

Citing a recent report commissioned by a group of African finance ministers, the Report says that the majority of countries in sub-Saharan Africa "now have lower capability, including state capability, than they did at independence".

While this is hardly a surprise to those with a close knowledge of the failure of African economic development since the mid-1970s, it is a startling admission on the part of the organisation at the heart of African economic policymaking and one that is certainly at odds with many of its earlier assessments, not least the much-discredited 1994 World Bank report, Adjustment in Africa.

This is why the 1997 report is so significant. It acknowledges two crucial points - that there is much more to the development process than getting policies right, difficult enough though that is, and secondly that development cannot be imposed from outside.

It is all very well for Zambia to hire British expatriates to launch its independent revenue authority and for Mozambique to employ British Crown Agents to run its customs service, but these are band-aids - short-term solutions. It is what happens after the technical experts have left that matters. Experience over the last 25 years shows that when the expatriates go they leave a vacuum.

Indeed, the Bank says as much: "An institutional vacuum of significant proportions has emerged in many parts of Sub-Saharan Africa, leading to increased crime and an absence of security, affecting investment and growth."

Diagnosis is far easier than cure. The World Bank is on the right track when it says most countries will need to redirect existing, but misallocated, resources. It calls for increased real wages for public servants - more than proportionately to any savings from further retrenchment - higher spending on social services, and urges governments to undertake "vast investments" in personnel management, retraining and accountability.

Just how all this is to be done while simultaneously cutting public sector deficits and rebuilding the physical - as well as the institutional - infrastructure is unclear. Predictably enough the Bank calls for more private-public sector co-operation to improve the delivery of public services but, as with the Crown Agents in Mozambique, this runs the risk of becoming a palliative not a solution.

The report shows that at headquarters, at least, the World Bank is learning from past mistakes. How long it will take to operationalise the message and ensure that other donors and agencies follow suit is another matter.

The IMF would be a good starting place. Advising Zimbabwe on deficit reduction, the Fund ignores the report's findings on crime, suggesting that the retrenchment in the army should be extended to the police. It wants civil servants to pay higher pension contributions - thereby reducing their real take-home pay - again directly contradicting its sister institution's advice.
In this situation, who are African finance ministers supposed to believe?
The Bank's call for real wages rises - more than in proportion to retrenchment savings - or the Fund's commitment to budget deficit reduction, regardless of the impact on institutional capability?

Of concern too is the nature of judgements on institutional capability. The Harare representative of the IMF is on record - in the South African media - as citing the refusal of backbench MPs to vote for a government guarantee for the new airport contract as evidence that governance in Zimbabwe is improving.

Threats to nationalise a foreign-owned mining company, the ongoing row over cellphone contracts, over the plundering of the war veterans fund, over the misuse of a government housing fund - are, it would seem, insignificant. This is just one more classic case of the Fund grasping desperately at straws in the face of a raft of contradictory evidence.

If the World Bank's survey responses mean anything at all, it is that judgments on governance, institutional capacity and policy credibility should be far more firmly and objectively-based. If they are not then the donor community will continue to undermine, rather than promote, the institutional capability without which there can be no African renaissance.
(The opinions expressed in this article represent those of the author only. They should not be seen to represent the views of Reuters.)
